questions.questionText: How does context engineering differ from prompt engineering?
options: They are exactly the same thing
Prompt engineering is about phrasing one instruction; context engineering is the broader discipline of deciding everything (and what to exclude) that goes into the context window
Context engineering only applies to image models
Context engineering replaces the need for a system prompt
questions.correctAnswer: Prompt engineering is about phrasing one instruction; context engineering is the broader discipline of deciding everything (and what to exclude) that goes into the context window
questions.explanation: Context engineering is the wider concern of what competes for the limited context budget across system instructions, history, retrieved documents, and tool definitions — not just how one instruction is worded.

questions.questionText: Why is selective retrieval described as context engineering's most impactful technique for knowledge-heavy applications?
options: It's the only technique that exists
Retrieving only the specific relevant chunks (instead of stuffing an entire knowledge base into context) directly addresses the hard token budget constraint
It removes the need for a context window entirely
It only matters for very short conversations
questions.correctAnswer: Retrieving only the specific relevant chunks (instead of stuffing an entire knowledge base into context) directly addresses the hard token budget constraint
questions.explanation: Since the context window is a hard limit, retrieving only what's relevant to the current query is what makes large knowledge bases usable at all within that constraint — the core idea RAG builds on.

questions.questionText: Why does an agent with many loosely-related tools have a real context engineering cost, even for tools it doesn't end up calling?
options: It doesn't — unused tool definitions are free
Every available tool's schema/description consumes context tokens on every single call, whether or not that tool is actually invoked
Tools are only listed in context after being called
This only applies to LangGraph specifically, not other frameworks
questions.correctAnswer: Every available tool's schema/description consumes context tokens on every single call, whether or not that tool is actually invoked
questions.explanation: Tool definitions occupy context budget just by being available to the model, which is a direct argument for narrower, specialized agents (fewer tools each) over one agent with many tools.
